houses.first_published_by: Ballu 1917: 175-186 (report on the 1916 season, printed Paris 1917; also in BCTH 1917: 292-300, not seen, cited from Germain 1969: 106); the baths, which Ballu then classed as public, were reported a year earlier in his report on 1915 (Journal officiel, 1916, cited in Ballu 1917: 175 n. 2, not seen; BCTH 1916: 239-242, not seen, cited from Germain 1969: 106)

houses.notes: Christofle calls this the large house discovered in 1916 north of the Capitol [Christofle 1930: 61-62]. Germain describes a vast building on the west side of a street that leaves the decumanus on a north-west to south-east line, bordering it for about a hundred metres with a width of twenty. Three entrances open on the street, two of them behind porticoes, and lead to three courts, the northern one giving access to baths in the north-west part, while a great gallery of 40 by 4 m runs along the whole west side [Germain 1969: 106]. The largest room, 10 by 14 m, opened on the gallery by three doors and was paved with a marine procession around a river god and, to the east, still-life medallions [Germain 1969: 109, 111]. Two more panels show river gods, one from the gallery with the words FLVMEN VAMACCVRA [Germain 1969: 106-107, 113]. Repairing walls in 1927-29, Christofle found a further mosaic, 1.50 m square, with a laurel wreath [Christofle 1930: 62]. Germain found it hard to see the building as a simple private house and thought its arrangements pointed to un usage collectif [Germain 1969: 106, 118]. Ballu cleared the house in 1916 between the small west baths found the year before and a building north of the Capitol then taken for a chapel, and describes the gallery, an atrium of 10.80 by 6 m with two porticoes of four bays and a wide door straight onto the street, which he thought unusual for an atrium, and an oecus of 15 by 10 m with four rooms along its north side [Ballu 1917: 175-179]. In 1925 soundings in the ground between the baths and the house found remains of the same period, joined to both without a break, so the baths belonged to the house, and the supposed chapel, with its apse and colonnade of five bays, was more likely a tablinum; the same report corrects the gallery to 40.15 m and describes the two rooms found between the baths and the house, one of them with a concrete basin, once later walls bonded with earth were cleared away [Ballu 1926: 35-37].

analysis.summary: The Large House North of the Capitol (Grande maison au Nord du Capitole) runs about a hundred metres along a street north of the Capitol, with private baths at the north end, two rooms cleared in 1925 with a concrete basin, the house of 1916 with its 40 m gallery, atrium and oecus, and at the south an apsed hall that Ballu first took for a chapel. houses.first_published_by: Christofle 1930: 58 (first report, campaign of 1927); full description Christofle 1930: 62-65
houses.key_references: Christofle 1930: 58, 62-65, 68, 76; Laghmouche 2024: Table 1, p. 224 (lists only the Grande maison to the north).
houses.notes: Christofle found this small house about thirty metres north of the north wall of the large house north of the Capitol, and describes an atrium with rooms on three sides. The atrium was still fully paved, and eight sandstone columns without bases, 2.35 m high, were found standing and carried the four porticoes. At the centre was a basin whose south slab was cut in steps so that the overflow fell as a cascade, and one of its pillars was grooved for the lead pipe that fed it [Christofle 1930: 62, 64]. The entrance was at the north-east angle, where a vestibule with a concrete floor sloping down from the street led to a stair of five steps. The rooms had concrete floors, and the finest, which Christofle calls the tablinum, lay on the south side, measured 6.40 by 5.40 m and opened on the axis of the court by a double door 1.95 m wide [Christofle 1930: 64]. He also reports a house cleared in 1927, 50 metres south of the Château d'eau, with the same paved atrium, basin and eight columns, without saying that it is this one [Christofle 1930: 58, 68].

houses.key_references: Ballu 1923a: 44, 47-53 (discovery and description), 54-55 (restoration), 55 (mosaic to Museum), 56-67 (finds); Ballu 1923b general report: 7; Ballu 1924: 45-46 (completion), 46-47 (restoration), 48-53 (mosaics A-E with drawings), plan of the house p. 43; Ballu 1926: 36, 45-46 (reservoir enclosure, intaglios); Ballu 1906: 18 (first soundings, walls not yet recognized); Christofle 1938: 428-429 (funerary caissons reused in a wall); Germain 1969: 81-85, fig. 10 (cat. 101-109), 143-157 passim; Rebuffat 1969: 678 no. 11; Rebuffat 1974: 497; Laghmouche 2024: Table 1, p. 224 (chapter 219-227); Lepelley 1981
houses.notes: Ballu found this house in 1922, when soundings west of the Filadelfes Baths led first to private baths and then to the house itself, and he finished clearing its south side in 1923 [Ballu 1923a: 47; Ballu 1924: 45-46]. He places it outside the city wall and gives its total area as 2,464 m², where Germain gives about 2,500 m² and counts about forty rooms [Ballu 1923a: 47; Germain 1969: 81]. The south front had five independent shops and two entrances, each with a two-column porch [Ballu 1923a: 47; Ballu 1924: 46]. The first part lay around a court of 21.55 by 10.05 m that Ballu calls the atrium, with a tablinum of 8.45 by 9.70 m off its west portico, a stair to an upper floor, and small private baths in the north-east corner [Ballu 1923a: 48-52]. The north portico and three rooms behind it had mosaics, and Germain assigns the floral ones probably to the early third century CE [Ballu 1923a: 49-50; Ballu 1924: 48-51; Germain 1969: 85]. The second court had fourteen columns on three sides and a central well, but the rooms around it were badly ruined [Ballu 1923a: 52]. A brick kiln, a pottery kiln and Christian children's graves came later [Ballu 1923a: 49, 53]. Rebuffat thought the room between the courts was probably a triclinium [Rebuffat 1969: 678].

analysis.summary: Ballu's two-part villa outside the city wall, the largest house he had found at Timgad (2,464 m², Ballu 1923a: 47), an atrium and a peristyle with the tablinum between them, a row of five shops on the street, each on its own, and a private bath suite in the north-east corner. On the round-2 drawing it is 66 spaces with 13 rings, a maximum depth of 10 and a mean depth of 3.44, the deepest house so far, and the secondary entrance brings a visitor to the atrium court in four steps and the main entrance in five, while the baths lie behind one narrow passage in the atrium's north-east corner, the laconicum ten steps from the street. The peristyle is two steps from outside through a threshold in its west wall, or five behind the south front alone.

houses.name: House of Sertius (Maison de Sertius)
houses.alternate_names: House of Marcus Plotius Faustus Sertius; House of Plotius Faustus et Cornelia Valentina Tucciana; Rebuffat no. 9
houses.area_raw: 2 263 m² (Ballu 1903: 81: 62 x 36.50 m; corroborated by Ballu 1923a: 47) against 3 600 m² (Germain 1969: 59, no dimensions given)
houses.first_published_by: Gsell 1902 (Rapport archéologique sur les fouilles faites en 1901, BCTH 1902): 315-316 (offprint pp. 10-11; first notice, the house of 'Faustus et Valentina'); first full description Ballu 1903: 81-89
houses.notes: This house north-west of the South Baths, cleared in 1900 and 1901, was first reported by Gsell and described in full by Ballu, who traced the original town wall running through it [Gsell 1902: 315-316; Ballu 1903: 10, 81-89]. Ballu gives a rectangle of 62 by 36.50 m, or 2,263 square metres, whereas Germain gives 3,600 m² [Ballu 1903: 81; Germain 1969: 59]. The main entrance, on the Cardo Maximus behind a portico of eight columns, led through a paved vestibule to Ballu's atrium, a court of 14 by 12 m with a long basin; steps at the end of the vestibule led to private baths, and Ballu attributed two further bath rooms to the servants [Ballu 1903: 83-84]. Beyond the tablinum, whose mosaic went to the museum, a stone-paved peristyle court held a basin with a carved marble bowl above a lower tank that Ballu read as a fish pond [Ballu 1903: 84-86]. A base from the baths reading Hygiae Aug(ustae) Faustus et Valentina led Vars to ask, and Ballu to conclude, that the owners were M. Plotius Faustus Sertius and his wife, donors of the market [Gsell 1902: 316; Ballu 1903: 88]. Germain dated the mosaics between the early third and early fifth centuries CE, and Christofle later listed an inscribed column-die from the peristyle [Germain 1969: 64; Christofle 1938: 445].

analysis.spaces_note: 48 rooms, 2 courts, 6 porticoes, 1 street portico
analysis.summary: Entered from the east street through a seven-column portico and a columned hall, the house runs on one axis across a twelve-column court to an open tablinum, with a second, deeper court and its apsed oecus to the west and rows of street-entered rooms on the north and south sides. The house was redrawn on confidence-graded layers in October 2026, which gives fifty-six spaces, thirteen street doors on four streets and seventeen circulation rings, so no single room controls the way in. The shops along the south street connect to each other and to the street but reach the house itself only through one uncertain door and one certain one, which keeps work on the outside of the block and the household behind it, and the tablinum and the oecus sit among the least integrated spaces, where Fisher's table expects reception rooms to sit.

analysis.spaces_note: 15 spaces drawn, 14 reached (the room north of 192 has no door on the sketch); the court and its four porticoes, and the hall's two parts, cut apart on their colonnade lines
analysis.summary: A house inside the Donatist episcopal quarter west of the Capitol, between the cathedral's east wall and the chapel, named for the Donatist bishop Optatus, whose name is in the mosaic inscription of the room off the west portico, *haec iubente sacerdote Dei Op[tato ...]* in Albertini's restoration (Germain 1969: 122, 126-127). The only plan is a fragment of Meunier's unpublished 1938 sketch; on the round-2 drawing it is a full peristyle of four colonnades round a court of about 10 by 10 m, a hall north of the court, the mosaic rooms on the west and a passage along the east side with the way in at the north-east corner from the complex's corridor, 15 spaces (14 reached) with 3 rings, a maximum depth of 5 and a mean depth of 2.93. The passage, not the court, is the hub, one step in; the court is three from the corner, or two by Meunier's uncertain south opening, and the three mosaic floors are the deepest decorated spaces, the west portico three steps in and the two rooms four and five, through the inscription room. Where the house's door really was, and what Meunier drew east and south of the fragment, stay open.

houses.alternate_names: Rebuffat no. 7; Entrepôt ou salle des ventes (Ballu 1911a: 49); Maison au sud de la porte de Lambèse (Germain 1969: 88)
houses.area_raw: ~1 725 m² (derived from 25 x 69 m, Ballu 1911a: 53 n. 1; not a published figure)
houses.first_published_by: Ballu, Rapport 1905, BCTH 1906: 201-204, pl. LVIII (offprint pp. 22-25); fuller treatment Ballu 1911a: 49-53, plan p. 51
houses.key_references: Ballu 1906: 201-204, pl. LVIII (further mentions 206-207 in the west-gate baths account)
houses.notes: First uncovered in 1905, the building stands 8 metres from the Lambèse gate on the south side of the decumanus, behind a portico of eight bays [Ballu, report on 1905, BCTH 1906: 201; Ballu 1911a: 49; Germain 1969: 88]. Ballu saw that the kerb before the widest bay had been worn by carts backing up to unload, and that a wide door led into a paved hall 10.40 m square [Ballu 1911a: 49]. Beyond lay a court of 12.50 by 20 m with a basin and porticoes on four sides, their stuccoed sandstone columns joined by stone slabs 1 m high. The south gallery, raised 1.50 m and paved in marble, opened through three doors onto a hall of 8.20 by 10.25 m with a fine mosaic and onyx-breccia wall panels. Ballu read this gallery as a platform for sales and the building, 25 by 69 m, as a warehouse and perhaps an auction hall [Ballu 1911a: 50-53]. Christofle, who finished the clearance and restoration, was inclined to see instead a complete Roman villa with an atrium and a second court, the peristylium, with four heated rooms of private baths south of it and a Medusa mosaic under its south portico [Christofle 1930: 58-62]. Rebuffat takes the west hall for the original triclinium and the south hall for one taken from a neighbouring house, and asks for a study of the alterations [Rebuffat 1969: 677].

analysis.summary: Behind an eight-bay portico on the Decumanus a cart door 3.26 m wide, with a smaller door beside it for people, opens into a square paved vestibule and through a second large door onto a great court whose colonnades were closed by stone slabs, with a raised gallery of green-veined marble and red breccia on its south side and behind it a hall that had a fine mosaic and onyx on its lower walls. The redrawn plan, traced from Christofle's plan of 1930 and checked against Ballu's of 1911, gives forty-eight spaces, fourteen street doors and twenty-six rings, with a maximum depth of four and a mean depth of 1.92. Inside the house the only way from the great court to the second court, Christofle's peristylium with its basin and the Medusa mosaic in a semicircular room at its corner, runs through that hall, while the rooms round the second court have street doors of their own on two sides, so the warehouse Ballu described and the villa Christofle described meet at a single room.

analysis.summary: A colonnaded portico on the Cardo fronts five double-depth shops, but the house itself is entered from the Voie des Thermes, through a vestibule and porter's lodge into a gallery the record gives as 30 m long and 7.30 m wide that opens through three bays into a hall with a big-cube mosaic, and only beyond the hall lies the court with its twenty-two columns, its late basin and its balustrades, with rooms on hypocausts north of the hall and the room of the hermaphrodite mosaic off the west portico. houses.notes: Fourth insula of the Decumanus row, 22.70 by 26 metres, bounded east by the street along the west wall of the Great East Baths. Five shops opened on the Decumanus and a staircase took over part of the east street. The house had a central court with a walk round it bounded by upright slabs set into stone blocks, and four rooms of private baths. houses.notes: First of the two fifth-row houses, level with the library and one file east of it, entered from the street on its south. A vestibule paved in sandstone, shaped at first like a corridor and then bending to the left, led by four steps to a paved atrium with a basin and its water pipe on the west side; a wide passage space to the right of the atrium and a portico in front of the tablinum both had mosaic floors, and the tablinum took its light from the street on the north. A sandstone latrine seat with three openings came from the room west of the tablinum. Off the vestibule's east side a narrow corridor led to a second, stone-paved atrium with an octagonal well, which had its own door on the east street; two stone troughs reused as mangers for the Byzantine cavalry lay on its wall with the large south-east corner room. In all, twelve rooms, two atria and a vestibule [Ballu 1905: 86-87; Ballu 1911a: 82-83; Inv. Mos. III, 135-136].

houses.notes: Ballu placed the entrance on the south, where a door two metres wide led to a vestibule paved in sandstone, with latrines to the right on entering and, to the left, a staircase of which seven steps survive and which led to an upper storey. Facing the door, an inner corridor paved in limestone, 3.55 m wide and 9.75 m long, gave access to all the rooms, and on its north side three intercolumniations opened onto an atrium paved in limestone (9.55 by 4.50 m), with a square well in its front part. The west wall of the tablinum kept traces of painted plaster imitating marbles of various colours. Ballu found large quantities of wheat and barley, blackened by fire but with the grains intact, and all the columns overturned near their bases, and he concluded from this that the house had been destroyed rapidly [Ballu 1911a: 72-76]. His two accounts differ on one point: the book puts the vestibule in the south-east angle of the house, the 1906 report in the south-west [Ballu 1911a: 72; Ballu, report on 1906, BCTH 1907: 261]. The house was drawn in GIS from the georeferenced plans and satellite imagery in August 2026. The drawing keeps an open question the sources disagree on: Wilson's plan puts the main street door on the east side, while Ballu describes it on the south, beside the staircase and latrines. The southern reading fits Ballu's description best, and both openings are recorded so the question stays visible.

houses.notes: Ballu lists this as the fourth of the isolated houses, facing the building he called the Schola across the northern Cardo Maximus, between the first and second decumanus, with the voie du Forum on its west side. On the Cardo Maximus it had a portico of five columns and two square piers. A wall running east to west divided it into two equal parts: the southern part had an atrium and six rooms, one of which kept a fragment of mosaic paving, and the northern part, which communicated with the southern through three wide doors, had six rooms. The room at the north-west corner held a mosaic that looked ordinary until cleaning on 7 May 1902 revealed Diana at her bath surprised by Actaeon, and Ballu had it moved at once to the museum because of its interest and the richness of its colours [Ballu 1903: 96-97]. Germain gives the room as 6.60 by 5 m, opening through three bays on two columns still in place, and the panel as 2.50 by 2.35 m. The inscription SELIV/S P G at the top of the panel was restored by Cagnat as the mosaicist's signature, Selius p(in)g(ebat), though Germain prefers p(in)g(it) or p(i)c(tor) [Germain 1969: 19-22].

houses.name: House of the Gardens (Jardinières) (Maison des Jardinieres)
houses.notes: Ballu described a house 21 m wide and 24 m deep on the Decumanus, with a street portico on eight square pillars of which only the footings remained. An opening of 2.10 m led to a vestibule, and two doors led from it to an atrium of 10.50 by 10.60 m with a portico of ten columns. A large stone planter ran around the paved centre, left open for 2.20 m on the side opposite the entrance, and double heads (bifrons), of tragic masks and other types, crowned its four stone uprights; the well was 10 m deep. Three bays on two columns opened onto the tablinum, and on each side a passage (fauces) led to a corner room (alae), these rooms closing the house on the south. Ballu noted that the house stood in a space reserved for public buildings and took it for the home of a magistrate or other important person [Ballu 1897b: 224-226]. The 1905 account gives an atrium about 10 m square, a portico 2 m wide with ten columns, four across and three deep, a well 9 m deep, geometric mosaics in brown and yellow under the porticoes and a geometric mosaic with plant ornament in the tablinum [BCB 1905: 88-92]. Germain calls its dimensions assez restreintes [Germain 1969: 37], and Ballu later reported that its columns had been set upright again [Ballu 1903: 110]. Placement note: Germain's plan sets this house in her insula 70, the block immediately east of the Forum on the south side of the Decumanus, and the georeferenced plan agrees, so the house is placed in that block from the neighbouring one north of the Decumanus.

analysis.summary: A single street door from the Decumanus leads through a vestibule onto a ten-column court whose porticoes open onto nine small rooms, with a three-bayed reception room on the entrance axis where the figured mosaic lies. The house was redrawn on confidence-graded layers in September 2026, which gives sixteen spaces reached from one entrance, with two circulation rings running through the porticoes. The court is square, with a well and planters rather than the semicircular atrium of the later plans, the tripartite front of the reception room is confirmed, and no room opens directly onto the street, which points to a single household without shops along the frontage.

houses.name: House of the Pool (Maison de la Piscina)
houses.alternate_names: fifteenth house in Ballu's 1903 list (Ballu 1903: 102, 'la quinzième'); BCB 1905 blocks (carrés) 73 and 82; later block numbering 67/75 (Rebuffat 1969: 676, 'Maison 67/75 (ex-73/82)'); Rebuffat no. 2
houses.first_published_by: Ballu 1897b (Les ruines de Timgad I): 228-230 [1903 notice at Ballu 1903: 102]
houses.notes: The Maison de la Piscina lies on the Decumanus Maximus, 12 metres east of the Arch of Trajan by Ballu's account [Ballu 1903: 81]. Its plot, which Ballu gave first as 20 by 50 metres and later as 20.80 by 50, joins two blocks of the original grid across a street that was built over [Ballu 1897b: 228; Ballu 1903: 102]. The half on the main street was largely destroyed, and while Ballu believed it held the main entrance and an atrium, the 1905 volume says its purpose cannot be told [Ballu 1897b: 228-229; BCB 1905: 333-334]. In the intact southern half Ballu recorded a peristyle whose open court measured 9.50 by 6.25 m, and an oecus of 6.30 by 6.73 m opening onto it through three unequal bays [Ballu 1897b: 229]. The basin that names the house, long with a half-round end, was of blue granite and carried nine pink marble columns 2.30 m high, and half the portico was lost in a rebuilding Ballu dated to the Byzantine period [Ballu 1897b: 229-230]. The 1905 volume calls the court an atrium and the south room a tablinum, and places baths with hypocausts in the north-east, while Rebuffat counts three porticoes and calls the room a triclinium [BCB 1905: 333-334; Rebuffat 1969: 676]. The oecus mosaic went to the museum, and Germain dated the fittings probably to the early third century CE [Ballu 1911a: 179; Germain 1969: 42-44].

analysis.spaces_note: 26 rooms, the court and its three porticoes; 29 reached, one small west room has no door on the plan
analysis.summary: The House of the Pool (Maison de la Piscina) joins two blocks of the grid across a street that was built over, with a destroyed front range on the Decumanus, a strip of rooms on the line of the old street and a peristyle block at the back, where a blue granite basin with nine columns stands in a court with porticoes on three sides and an oecus with a three-bay front and mosaic 44 closes the axis. Redrawn on the graded layers (Sep 30, 2026): thirty spaces, ten street doors on three streets, fourteen rings, the east portico the most integrated space and the oecus deep and single-sided, with a side door into a small lobby for service.

houses.name: Ballu 1903 House 16 (La seizième)
houses.notes: Ballu lists this as the sixteenth of the isolated houses, bounded on the east by the voie de la Curie, on the south by the second decumanus, on the west by the southern Cardo Maximus and on the north by the first decumanus, and measuring 20.40 by 20.65 m. He thought it had been occupied by two families, separated by a wall running north to south, although the two parts communicated. The eastern part had seven rooms, two of them antechambers opening on the first and second decumanus, and the western part had four rooms and a long vestibule (12.80 m) opening on the second decumanus [Ballu 1903: 102].
